Peer reviewers reject this, stating the patch clamp data are 'of very poor quality,' questioning whether results represent 'leak currents,' noting 'Trpm2-/- controls are missing,' and that '20 uM ACA is not a selective inhibitor.'

Both address ER→lysosome Ca2+ flux (C77-C81). OpenEval finds strong support from GEM-CEPIA1er and D1ER measurements showing temporal correlation. Peer reviewers fundamentally reject this, stating 'ER-Lysosome Ca2+ refilling experiments rely on transient transfection' which is 'highly problematic,' and 'the data procured are also not convincing and lack critical controls.'

Both evaluate IP3R involvement in ER→lysosome Ca2+ transfer (C82-C88). OpenEval finds support from Xestospongin C and TPEN effects. Peer reviewers reject the underlying ER-lysosome Ca2+ refilling data due to transfection issues and lack of controls, undermining these mechanistic claims.

Both address VAPA-ORP1L contacts facilitating Ca2+ refilling (C89-C90). OpenEval finds PLA data supportive though mechanistic link not directly tested. Peer reviewers' rejection of the ER-lysosome Ca2+ refilling approach extends to questioning these contact site data.

Both evaluate SOCE activation and its role in inflammasome (C91-C98). OpenEval finds support from pharmacological inhibitors and D1ER measurements. Peer reviewers state 'there is no credible evidence that SOCE is activated,' criticizing 'snapshot measurements and crude non-selective inhibitors,' and stating 'the only definitive way' is patch clamp electrophysiology.

Both address STIM1-ORAI1 colocalization as evidence of SOCE (C99-C101). OpenEval finds confocal microscopy data supportive. Peer reviewers' rejection of SOCE activation evidence extends to questioning whether these colocalization data demonstrate functional SOCE in this context.

Major disagreement on histological nerve regeneration evidence (C7, C99-C101, C120-C127). OpenEval finds the immunofluorescence data supportive, but peer reviewers explicitly state 'The histological data and analyses following spinal cord injury are not convincing' citing poor image quality and resolution insufficient to support quantitative claims.

Both evaluate the simulation protocol (C22, C35-C41). OpenEval finds the design well-controlled with validation demonstrating comparable conformational sampling. Peer reviewers fundamentally challenge comparability, stating the short apo simulations (1-4 μs) are insufficient for meaningful conformational transitions in a 140-residue IDP, making direct comparison with the 1500 μs fasudil dataset invalid for MSM construction.

Both evaluate the MSM finding of increased metastable states (C49-C51). OpenEval finds this supported by Chapman-Kolmogorov validation and control analyses. Peer reviewers fundamentally reject the MSM validity, stating insufficient conformational transitions in short apo simulations make the kinetics and thermodynamics 'relatively meaningless' and comparisons with fasudil MSM 'likely to be meaningless.'

Both address trajectory length validation (C52-C53). OpenEval considers the control analyses adequate to rule out artifacts. Peer reviewers dismiss this validation, maintaining that the fundamental issue of insufficient conformational transitions in short apo simulations remains unaddressed regardless of these controls.

Both evaluate protein entropy calculations (C99-C106). OpenEval finds MIST approach sound with clear demonstration of entropy range broadening and correlation with populations. Peer reviewers reject these conclusions, stating that entropy analysis depends entirely on valid macrostates, which are fundamentally questioned, making entropy differences and their interpretation as fasudil-induced modulation unsupported.

Both address residue-wise entropy analysis (C107-C118). OpenEval finds correlation between binding sites and entropy changes clearly demonstrated. Peer reviewers reject this as unsupported because the fundamental MSM critique means 'kinetics and thermodynamics of the resulting MSM are likely to be relatively meaningless,' invalidating entropy-based conclusions.

Both evaluate MFPT analysis and kinetic slowing (C120-C127). OpenEval finds the correlation between entropy and transition times clearly demonstrated with reasonable mechanistic interpretation. Peer reviewers explicitly reject this, stating that if simulations are too short for conformational transitions (likely for apo dataset), 'any kinetics and thermodynamics modeled by an MSM will be inherently meaningless.'

Both address the main entropy expansion conclusion (C128). OpenEval finds it well-supported by MSM and entropy analyses, though noting rigorous demonstration would require total ensemble entropy calculation. Peer reviewers directly challenge this central conclusion, stating comparisons are 'likely to be meaningless' due to fundamental simulation/analysis flaws, with editor noting 'simulations and analyses in their present form are inadequate.'

Both discuss entropy-expansion mechanism context (C90-C91). OpenEval finds the interpretation reasonable given observed states and conformational space. Peer reviewers reject the entropy-expansion mechanism as unsupported, stating that without valid MSMs and thermodynamic analysis, this mechanistic conclusion cannot be sustained.

Both address attention paradigm validation (C55-C58, C61-C62). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED by data in Figures 4-6 with established alpha-band phenomena, though notes additional activations remain suggestive. Peer reviewers find UNSUPPORTED: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'no actual comparison appears to have been completed' with standard EEG analysis despite abstract claims, calling refusal to compare 'illogical.' Major disagreement on whether comparison was actually performed.

Both address characterization of SPECTRE vs source localization differences (C82-C84, C88-C92). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED though notes LoretaKey1 comparison somewhat unfair. Peer reviewers find UNSUPPORTED: Reviewer 1 explicitly rejects authors' justification for not comparing, calling it 'illogical,' and Reviewer 3 notes 'comparisons to benchmark remain unaddressed.' Major disagreement on whether fundamental differences justify avoiding validation comparisons.

Both evaluate negative results for MBK-2 involvement (C83-C94). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, viewing the comprehensive negative evidence as strong. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, stating they are 'left unconvinced' and noting missing data, unreliable RNAi in neurons, and insufficient evidence for the negative conclusion. Major disagreement on adequacy of negative evidence.

Both evaluate the comparative performance claims (C5, C6, C38-C44) from Table 1. OpenEval finds the results SUPPORTED with caveats about true negative definitions, while peer reviewers find them UNSUPPORTED, explicitly stating the FTMap comparison is invalid because FTMap identifies small molecule binding sites, not PPI hot spots. This represents a fundamental disagreement on the validity of the performance comparison.

Both address speed-accuracy tradeoff absence and reflex-speed claims (C8, C79, C110, C120). OpenEval finds it SUPPORTED with no correlation between error and latency. Peer review rates it UNSUPPORTED - Reviewer 2 explicitly challenges the 40ms claim as having 'little support,' noting previous studies show 60-75ms latencies, and criticizes mentioning 40ms in abstract as 'overselling the result.'

Both evaluate molecular subtyping claims (C34-C38, with OpenEval also covering C78-C79). OpenEval finds the approach biologically-informed with significant survival differences and appropriate methodology. Peer reviewer R3 explicitly states the subtype results are 'not convincing,' noting univariate analysis is insufficient and that lack of multivariable analysis means authors cannot claim clinically relevant subtypes. Strong disagreement on subtype validity.

Both evaluate novelty and clinical promise claims (C45, C88-C91, C94). OpenEval finds the radiomics-EV miRNA integration methodologically innovative and well-documented, though notes C94's clinical promise is aspirational. Peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, with editor stating evidence is incomplete, R3 identifying fundamental design flaws, and R2 calling the design flawed, making broad clinical claims premature. Major disagreement on novelty and clinical utility.

Both evaluate pathway enrichment analysis (C42-C44, C66). OpenEval finds the GSEA methodology standard and appropriate with clear presentation. Peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED because the pathway analyses are downstream of unconvincing subtype classification, with R3's critique about insufficient multivariable analysis applying to all functional characterization. Disagreement stems from different assessments of upstream subtyping validity.

Partial claim overlap (C7, C75-C76). Major disagreement: OpenEval rates main causal conclusion as SUPPORTED with converging evidence from multiple measures. Peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, explicitly challenging the causal claim and stating 'results still do not lead to the conclusion that the angular gyrus is causally involved' due to absence of target engagement analyses.

Both evaluate the Scott-Hwa computational model (C24-C30, C54). OpenEval finds the model well-supported with clear mechanistic explanations. Peer reviewers explicitly reject this, arguing the bacterial model is inappropriate for yeast due to missing ppGpp regulation and lack of quantitative validation in yeast. This is a major disagreement on model applicability.

Both evaluate the Weisse model (C32-C36). OpenEval finds it supported with clear computational results demonstrating the Product function. Peer reviewers explicitly challenge this, noting the model was only fitted to E. coli data and never validated for yeast, questioning its applicability to explain genome-wide patterns. Strong disagreement on model validity.

Both address limitations of the Product function for beneficial mutations (C31, C59-C60). OpenEval views this as an appropriately noted boundary condition. Peer reviewers include these claims in their broader critique of the Scott-Hwa model's applicability, viewing them as part of an unsupported mechanistic framework.

Both evaluate mechanistic explanations for deviations (C37, C39). OpenEval finds the analytical approximation and identification of nonlinear kinetics well-supported. Peer reviewers reject the underlying models, arguing they fail to account for the generality of product neutrality across diverse genetic perturbations.

Strong disagreement on telomere silencing effectiveness (C61). OpenEval treats this as supported contextual claim from literature. However, Peer Reviewer 3 explicitly challenges the silencing claim with data showing nonsignificant differences and reduced expression in SY12 strain, directly contradicting the interpretation.

Strong disagreement on predictive conclusion about 3'UTR regulation (C8, C121). OpenEval finds the prediction reasonable given the data, appropriately acknowledging it as hypothesis requiring validation. Peer reviewers explicitly challenge this conclusion, stating there is 'little proof that the results have biological significance' and 'insufficient orthogonal validation.' Editor concludes evidence is incomplete.

Both evaluate behavioral evidence for IR-induced cognitive impairment (C3, C13-C16). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED with multiple validated tests and statistical significance. Peer review finds it UNSUPPORTED due to fundamental flaws: inappropriate timing (3-8 days vs required >2 months), inappropriate dose fractionation (5x2 Gy too protective), marginal effects, low sample sizes (4-5 animals), and methodological issues with habituation and exploration levels.

Both evaluate in vivo antagomiR therapeutic efficacy (C8, C50-C55, with OpenEval also including C89, C93). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with evidence of brain delivery, target engagement, and behavioral rescue. Peer review finds UNSUPPORTED because the baseline cognitive impairment at 3-8 days is 'completely irrelevant' per Reviewer 2, making rescue of this non-physiological phenotype invalid; Reviewer 1 also requests in vivo molecular marker staining.

Major disagreement on SF profile-category relationship (C23-C58 vs C21-C59). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with novel evidence from quadratic fitting and separability index. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, stating 'The conclusion that single-unit spatial frequency selectivity can predict object coding requires further evidence' and findings are 'premature given the low number of stimuli.'

Disagreement on population-level SF-category correlation (C21-C22, C59). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with high correlations (0.66, 0.39) and significant p-values. Peer reviewers challenge this as part of their broader UNSUPPORTED assessment of the SF-category predictive relationship, citing insufficient evidence.

Strong disagreement on stimulus duration (C125). OpenEval finds methodological details SUPPORTED as enabling reproducibility. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, identifying 'One big issue' that 'stimulus duration was too brief and could have weakened the effects of high spatial frequencies and confounded the conclusions.'

Major disagreement on IR expression patterns (C43, C44, C45). OpenEval finds the immunohistochemistry data for IR56d supportive, but peer reviewers identify critical contradictions with multiple previous studies showing IR56d in sweet neurons, not bitter neurons. Peer review also notes lack of adult expression for Ir7g and Ir51b GAL4 reporters.

Strong disagreement on C31. OpenEval finds the control experiment with unfamiliar mice appropriately validates social vs. non-social factors (SUPPORTED), while Peer Reviewer 3 explicitly challenges this claim as false, providing statistical reasoning that mice did not perform at chance and questioning whether individual identification is necessary (UNSUPPORTED).

Both address control analyses for confounding variables (C65-C68, C143). OpenEval finds the controls appropriate and strengthening (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers find them inadequate. Reviewer 2 states the movement analysis is 'unconvincing' and 'I see no effort by the authors to investigate the importance of movement and motivation' (UNSUPPORTED).

Both address novelty claims (C104). OpenEval rates connectivity findings as SUPPORTED with justified novelty claim, while peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, explicitly stating 'claims of primacy in showing early prefrontal cortical involvement...several studies already have shown this,' rejecting the novelty claim.

Major disagreement on core findings (C10, C11, C42, C43). OpenEval rates as UNSUPPORTED due to failure of Bonferroni correction, marginal associations, and lack of replication. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, describing 'convincing evidence' for three immune cell types. This represents the most significant divergence in the evaluations.

Strong disagreement on MVMR and sensitivity analyses (C17, C18, C76, C77). OpenEval rates as UNSUPPORTED, citing internal contradictions and lack of robustness as undermining causal claims. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting these as part of careful methodological rigor.

Strong disagreement on therapeutic target claims (C44). OpenEval rates as UNSUPPORTED, stating gene targets are speculative and conclusions overstate evidence strength. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting translational interpretation within context of overall findings.

Major disagreement on clinical implications (C47, C85, C86). OpenEval rates as UNSUPPORTED, calling translational claims premature and inconsistent with study limitations. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, with one explicitly affirming 'significant implications for periodontal care.'

Strong disagreement on epistasis interpretation (C91-C94). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED while acknowledging alternative interpretations are possible. Peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 explicitly stating 'the claim that dact1/2 function downstream of wnt11f2 is not well supported' due to distinct expression patterns and likely secondary effects.

Agreement on acknowledging limitations (C170-C171). Both evaluations note the importance of acknowledging that capn8 necessity was not tested. OpenEval rates these limitation statements as appropriately SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers emphasize these limitations more strongly in their UNSUPPORTED rating of functional claims.

Both address visual inspection of pRF maps (C61). OpenEval considers this part of converging evidence supporting the claims. Peer review explicitly challenges this as UNSUPPORTED, with Reviewer 2 stating they disagree that differences are 'clear' and suggesting the visualization method is inadequate. This is a direct disagreement on the interpretability of the visual data.

Both evaluate BLI binding data (C92-C95). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, viewing BLI as resolving MST discrepancies and avoiding fluorescent labeling artifacts. Peer review rates as UNSUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 arguing BLI results are inconsistent with published literature, show poor sensorgram fits, and may be subject to artifacts.

OpenEval supports claims C38 and C73 regarding FtsW mutant suppression, while peer reviewers rate this UNSUPPORTED, explicitly stating that the spotting assay shows only FtsB-E56A and FtsA-E202K provide full rescue, and that claims about FtsW-M254I and S274G are misleading.

OpenEval supports claim C67 as part of a summary of key findings, while peer reviewers rate claims involving C67 (regarding FtsW suppression) as UNSUPPORTED, stating that FtsW mutants do not provide full rescue comparable to complementation.

Partial overlap on background/context claims. OpenEval R16 evaluates extensive background literature (C1-C2, C14-C33, C53-C55, C96, C116-C153) as appropriately cited context. Peer review R9 challenges subset of these claims (C2, C17, C29, C139-C147) specifically regarding clinical stress and translational relevance, finding them unsupported by human evidence.

Both evaluate the main conclusion (C73, C82-C83) about mTOR balance regulating sperm epigenetic aging. OpenEval finds convergent evidence from bidirectional genetic manipulation well-supports the conclusion, though notes the complete molecular cascade isn't established. Peer reviewers rate this UNSUPPORTED, with Reviewer 3 stating the central hypothesis 'appears irrelevant or invalid' due to lack of chronologically old animals and adequate controls. Editor concludes evidence is incomplete.

Minor overlap on C84. OpenEval R7 includes C84 among phenotypic changes supporting the hypothesis. Peer R10 addresses main conclusions including C84, finding them unsupported due to fundamental experimental design flaws and lack of chronologically old animals.

Both evaluate claims C33-C35 about microglia DEGs and AD genetics. OpenEval finds these SUPPORTED by citations and reanalysis data, while peer review rates them UNSUPPORTED, expressing concern that 'almost all DEGs found by the authors are in the rare cell types' and noting unconvincing supporting literature and potential false positives driven by outliers.

Strong disagreement on main conclusions (C6, C119). OpenEval finds conclusions supported by consistent evidence across analyses, noting small effect sizes as a caveat. Peer reviewers explicitly challenge the 'general physiological mechanism' conclusion, stating effect sizes are too small (< 0.10) to support such broad claims.

Both address dating claims (C89-C102) but reach opposite conclusions. OpenEval finds the dating approach 'methodologically sound but indirect' and appropriately conservative (SUPPORTED). Peer reviewers explicitly reject it as UNSUPPORTED, stating there is 'no direct or closely associated chronometric dating' and the chronological context is 'physically so far removed from these rock markings, as to be misleading at best.' This represents a fundamental disagreement on whether indirect dating via associated skeletal remains is acceptable.

Both address authorship attribution to H. naledi (C82-C88, C68-C69). OpenEval finds the exclusivity documentation and proximity of remains SUPPORTED though 'circumstantial.' Peer reviewers explicitly reject this as UNSUPPORTED and 'premature,' emphasizing that 'juxtaposition' does not demonstrate authorship and that 'this landscape has been home to multiple hominins.' Major disagreement on whether spatial association constitutes adequate evidence.

Both address methodological documentation (C130-C139) with identical claim sets. OpenEval finds methods SUPPORTED as 'appropriate for documentation' though preliminary. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, criticizing the lack of 'image enhancements - which is standard in most rock art research' and noting that advanced imaging techniques used at sites like Blombos are 'not invasive or destructive' and should have been employed. Disagreement on methodological adequacy.

Minor overlap on exclusivity claims (C68-C69). OpenEval includes these in SUPPORTED systematic ruling out of alternatives. Peer reviewers explicitly reject authorship attribution as UNSUPPORTED. The exclusivity of H. naledi presence vs. authorship attribution represents different aspects that lead to divergent conclusions.

Major disagreement on auto/alloimmunity claims (C133, C135). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED as interpretive conclusion based on combined data from current and previous work. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, explicitly challenging that 'no data that supports this statement is shown' in current work and requiring proper citation if referring to previous publications.

Disagreement on sepsis definition context (C1, C6, C7). OpenEval rates these background claims as SUPPORTED, describing them as appropriately cited literature context. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, stating 'the definition of sepsis is outdated' and that Sepsis-3 definition must be used instead of SIRS-based Sepsis-2 framework.

Potential disagreement on statistical threshold (C57). OpenEval rates UNSUPPORTED, criticizing p<0.2 as unusually permissive and increasing false positive risk. Peer reviewers rate mass spectrometry findings SUPPORTED without specifically addressing this statistical concern.

Both address claims about extending current knowledge (C118-C119). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED based on high-sensitivity detection and brain-wide analysis. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, directly challenging that the methodology extends knowledge, noting other studies have achieved similar or better resolution and specificity.

Both address alternative MCM loading mechanisms (C134-C141). OpenEval finds inference of alternative mechanism logical given data. Peer reviewers explicitly challenge this, stating 'Biochemically, ORC without the ORC1 or ORC2 subunits cannot load the MCM helicase' and 'we still have no information about an alternative pathway,' showing fundamental disagreement.

Both assess evidence against incomplete deletion (C145-C147). OpenEval finds high EYFP penetrance and undetectable protein provide strong evidence but acknowledges Western blot limits. Peer reviewers remain skeptical, stating 'not all hepatocytes have the ORC1 and ORC2 genes deleted' and noting Western blots have 'non-linear response curves,' showing significant disagreement.

Both evaluate main conclusion about ORC-independent replication (C153-C154, C11). OpenEval finds data strongly supportive. Peer reviewers explicitly challenge this, with multiple stating they 'find the conclusion somewhat hard to accept' and that 'it remains possible that small amounts of residual ORC are responsible,' showing fundamental disagreement on the paper's central claim.

Both address inability to prove absolute absence of ORC (C157). OpenEval finds the caveat appropriate and notes evidence makes absence 'progressively unlikely.' Peer reviewers emphasize this limitation more strongly, stating 'the authors cannot confirm that it is deleted in all cells,' both acknowledging the limitation but with different weight.

Major disagreement on generalizability claims (C64). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, noting multi-ancestry approach represents important contribution; peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, stating 'their conclusion on generalizability of the maternal smoking risk score is currently not supported by their data.'

Disagreement on conclusions about South Asian populations (C67-C68). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED though notes interpretation requires careful consideration of confounding; peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED due to inability to validate in sufficient numbers of South Asian smokers.

Partial overlap on MRS portability across populations (C104). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with caution about lack of active smokers; peer reviewers included in UNSUPPORTED evaluation, stating 'the overall statement that smoking-associated MRS are portable across populations are not fully supported.'

OpenEval R11 addresses the central conceptual conclusion about TSE and entropic barriers (C44-C45, C58, C61) rated SUPPORTED. Peer R9 addresses C58 specifically and rates UNSUPPORTED, stating that demonstrating this as a 'catalytic strategy' requires comparison to non-enzymatic reaction that was not performed. Major disagreement on the fundamental claim.

Disagreement on absence of clinical disease (C85-C86, C124, C180). OpenEval rates this as SUPPORTED (well-documented limitation), while peer reviewers rate as UNSUPPORTED, explicitly identifying 'lack of phenotype' as a significant weakness that undermines the model's disease relevance.

Moderate claim overlap (C48-C50, C89) on bidirectional methylation fluctuation. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, viewing evidence of no fully demethylated neurons and tumor data as supporting bidirectional fluctuation that can be modeled. Peer review rates UNSUPPORTED, emphasizing that 'unstable nature of CpG methylation would introduce significant problems in inferring true cell lineage' and that fluctuating methylation contradicts fundamental requirement for stable inheritance.

Small overlap (C53, C54) on limitations and confounding factors. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED as honest assessment of limitations, noting untested assumptions and potential post-differentiation remodeling confounds. Peer review (within R7) rates UNSUPPORTED, using these same limitations as evidence that methylation patterns are fundamentally unreliable for lineage tracing.

Minimal overlap (C13, C25) but both address core conceptual validity. OpenEval rates methylation hierarchy findings SUPPORTED. Peer review rates UNSUPPORTED, fundamentally challenging the conceptual foundation: 'DNA methylation is unstable across cell divisions and differentiation, and is hardly called barcodes' and 'use of Human Brain Barcodes in the title lacks convincing evidence.' Editor notes 'evidence supporting claims remains incomplete.'

Significant disagreement. OpenEval evaluates claims C77-C90 as SUPPORTED, citing domain deletion, co-IP, and AlphaFold2 modeling. Peer review evaluates overlapping claims (C80-C82, C85-C86, C88-C90) as UNSUPPORTED, stating TM domain claims rely on structural simulation without direct biochemical validation of TM-TM interactions.

Both evaluate the quantitative c-di-AMP threshold estimate (C38, C135). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED as reasonable inference from comparing levels at different timepoints. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, noting strains with c-di-AMP around 300 pg/mL show effects while strains at 4000 pg/mL sometimes show no effects, and that 'only very high levels make a difference,' undermining the threshold model.

Both address the synthesis of evidence for TIP causality (C157-C158, C13, C53). OpenEval finds this SUPPORTED by multiple lines of evidence but acknowledges it remains an inference. Peer reviewers find this UNSUPPORTED, explicitly stating that 'linkage is just that, not definitive evidence' and that transgenic experiments would be needed for convincing proof.

Both evaluate major conclusions about extreme rearrangement and morphological conservation (C9-C11). OpenEval finds these well-supported by extensive genomic data contrasted with morphological conservation. Peer reviewer directly challenges these claims, stating they are 'unconvinced' the data 'justify the implications of the title or the claims made in the Summary' and noting insufficient justification that the pace is 'in any way remarkable.'

Both address predation/visibility arguments as limitations (C151, C154-C155). OpenEval finds authors appropriately acknowledge limitations and provide evidence that some factors are unlikely confounds. Peer reviewer explicitly challenges the predation/visibility argument as unconvincing, providing contrary evidence about visual signal requirements and predator-prey acoustic dynamics.

Strong disagreement on claim C29. OpenEval rates as UNSUPPORTED, identifying it as contradicting data in C16-C26 and likely a typographical error. Peer review groups C29 with C22-C28 and rates all as SUPPORTED, describing the fiber remodeling findings as validated without noting the contradiction.

Strong disagreement on claims C55-C58 regarding FAP proportions. OpenEval rates as UNSUPPORTED due to contradictory directional statements (increases described as decreases and vice versa), calling results 'uninterpretable.' Peer review groups with broader FAP claims (C59-C64) and rates as SUPPORTED, explicitly validating the conclusion that 'conjugated linoleic acid induces FAPs towards adipogenic commitment.'

OpenEval evaluates modeling framework definitions (C20-C22, C86-C89) as SUPPORTED, noting clear statements and explicit assumptions. Peer reviewers rate the modeling assumptions (C86, C87) as UNSUPPORTED, with Reviewer 3 explicitly challenging the assumption that plasmids don't affect each other and expressing concern about biological realism ('same cell counted in different pij runs counter to all intuition').
